title: HTML is All You Need (for Agents to Make Graphics) - Amol Kapoor, Nori

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is coding agents generating visual artifacts via HTML code generation as their core output modality. It presents a developer tooling principle for AI builders and applies it to enterprise workflows like board decks and sales materials. Nori is a production product using HTML-based agent graphics generation in real enterprise settings. summary: Amol Kapoor, CEO of Nori Atentic, presents the case that coding agents are far more capable than their reputation suggests, particularly for creating visual artifacts like slides, docs, and videos. The core problem is not that agents lack spatial reasoning but that they're given the wrong tools. Traditional design tools—PowerPoint, Figma, Canva—are built for human hands and eyes, relying on click, drag, and drop interactions matching human geospatial thinking. When agents use these tools via MCPs, CLIs, or screenshot loops, output is consistently poor: overlapping elements, invisible text, no alignment. Skeptics point to benchmarks like ARC-AGI and Simon Willison's SVG pelican-on-a-bicycle test as proof models can't reason about space. Amol counters that SVG is a wall of numbers even humans can't handwrite—asking an AI to manipulate a canvas is as mismatched as asking a human to write raw SVG. The mismatch is in the medium, not the model. HTML is the solution. Models have trained on billions of HTML examples and intuitively understand its structure. HTML tags carry semantic meaning (heading, chart, grid), the browser handles pixel rendering, and the model never places a coordinate. The same pelican test in HTML produces results the model can reason about and humans can read, theme, and edit. Amol emphasizes the editing format of a deck is arbitrary—audiences only see presentation mode. Nori uses HTML for all slide decks, board decks, sales decks, docs, and even the video itself. For end-to-end creation, agents can access company data like call transcripts and emails. Nori Sessions enables this, letting Amol build board decks from his phone during a subway commute. The key takeaway: stop thinking like a user, think like the model, and for graphics, all you need is HTML.

sections.title: Introduction and the Visual Artifact Problem
sections.summary: Amol introduces Nori, an AI employee that understands company data. He argues coding agents can do almost anything if you think like an agent. The world spends enormous time making slide decks, mostly on fiddling with formatting rather than thinking. Traditional tools like PowerPoint, Figma, and Canva are built for human hands and eyes with click-drag-drop patterns, but agents using these tools produce garbage output with overlapping elements and no alignment.

sections.title: SVG Pelican Test and the Medium Argument
sections.summary: Skeptics cite ARC-AGI and Simon Willison's SVG pelican-on-a-bicycle test as proof agents can't reason about space. Models produce genuinely bad SVG results. Amol counters that it's not the model but the medium: humans can't handwrite SVG either since it's a wall of numbers. Tools like Figma MCPs and PowerPoint CLIs all approach the problem like a human, but AI is not human.

sections.title: HTML as the Solution
sections.summary: Amol proposes HTML as the ideal medium: models have trained on billions of examples, understand it intuitively, and it renders to pixels everywhere. HTML tags carry semantic meaning (heading, chart, grid), letting the model think in structure without placing coordinates. The pelican test redone in HTML produces structured, editable, themeable results. The editing format of a deck is arbitrary—audiences only see presentation mode.

sections.title: Practical Applications at Nori
sections.summary: Nori uses HTML for all slide decks, board decks, sales decks, docs, and even the video itself—just divs all the way down. Plain text is usually the wrong choice when creating something useful. However, a beautiful deck alone is worthless without content. Giving agents access to company data like call transcripts and emails enables end-to-end deck creation. Nori Sessions allows Amol to build board decks from his phone during a subway commute.

sections.title: Conclusion and Key Takeaway
sections.summary: Amol wraps up with the core message: stop thinking like a user, think like the model. Give it the right language, and for graphics, all you need is HTML. Nori ships with everything needed to make this work, so there's no need to reinvent the wheel.
